newsitem.title: UK: London's FTSE rebounds above key 4,000 mark.
newsitem.headline: London's FTSE rebounds above key 4,000 mark.

text.p: London's FTSE 100 index rebounded to move decisively back above the psychological 4,000 mark in late Friday trade after three days of Wall Street-inspired jitters which saw the Dow Jones index dip under 6,000 overnight.
The index fell to a low of 3,981.8 earlier in the session, but traders mostly said the background remained positive after share markets' record run this year.
The bounce was helped by steady bonds and came amid hopes that cash-rich institutions would use recent declines as an opportunity to increase their equity holdings.
The FTSE 100 was up 23.7 points at 4,023.1 by 1417 GMT.

Market strategists said a faltering U.S. stock market could the wind out of London and other European shares again next week. But any setback in the UK is expected to be modest with dealers confident that sustained weakness will merely draw more money into the equities from cash-rich institutional investors.
Some traders said they expected investment institutions, carrying an estimated eight percent cash after recent strong dividends and share buybacks, to pump cash into the market.
"You will have nervous bouts from time to time but there are too many people out there sitting with surplus cash," said the head of equity trading at one leading brokerage.

"I don't think people are dramatically bearish," said one dealer. "There's still a favourable technical background and cash flow remains quite good, that's why I don't think there's a huge amount of downside."
Still, higher bond yields could undermine stocks. "Yields on gilts look set to break up above eight percent and that's becoming a real worry," the dealer said.
Others say shares are poised for a more substantial fall of the sort common in October, the month of the 1987 crash.
Robin Griffiths, chart analyst at HSBC James Capel, warned this week the FTSE 100 could drop 240 points in the short to medium term, though the longer-term bull trend remained intact.
Griffiths does not expect the market to peak until the early part of next year.

Richard Jeffrey, strategist at Charterhouse Tilney, said, "There's nervousness on a number of issues. One of them is Wall Street. Another is the domestic economy and whether rates are going to go up or ought to go up. The market has run out of momentum and it is quite easily spooked at the moment."

Jeffrey, who puts the possibility of an interest rate rise in Britain after next week's monthly monetary meeting on October 30 at 50-50, believes an early hike in rates would benefit markets long term.
"Shares may have an adverse reaction initially but it would help reassure people that the government's not going to let things get out of hand."
The health of the U.S. economy, however, is once again set to dominate in the short term, with U.S. jobs figures next Friday topping the agenda in a packed U.S. diary next week.
Friday also sees the release of U.S. leading indicators, factory goods and both the U.S. and UK purchasing managers indices. U.S income and spending data is out on Thursday.
Inflationary pressures may be muted at the moment but if interest rates are left at present levels, the concern is that problems may surface further down the line.
"The next two to three months might be OK, it's after that people will have to worry," said Nomura strategist Allison Southey.
"Whoever wins the next (UK) election is probably going to have to raise rates as soon as they get in because they're being held at present levels too long."
Strategists' year-end targets for the FTSE 100 range between 4,200 down to Nomura's 3,600, with many bunched around the 4,000 mark.
